questions.title: Dictionaries practice 1
questions.explanation: Updating `pen` does not create a second key. Adding `book` makes two keys total, and the current value stored under `pen` is 3.

questions.title: Dictionaries practice 2
questions.prompt: Which loop prints both each course name and its grade?
choices: for course, grade in grades.items():
for course, grade in grades:
for grade in grades.values, course:
for item in grades.keys().values():
questions.explanation: `items()` produces key-value pairs that can be unpacked into two variables. Iterating over the dictionary alone produces only keys.

questions.title: Trace Dictionaries
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
questions.explanation: Keys appear before colons and values appear after them. Square brackets use a key to find its value. The resulting output is "Ada\n{'name': 'Ada', 'credits': 18, 'major': 'CS'}".

questions.title: Dictionaries practice 5
questions.prompt: What does `scores.get("exam", 0)` return when "exam" is not a key?
choices: 0, the supplied default
None
It raises a KeyError
An empty string
questions.explanation: `get` returns the second argument when the key is missing, so this prints 0. `scores["exam"]` would raise a KeyError instead. With no default, `get` returns `None`, but here a default of 0 was given, so 0 is what comes back.

questions.title: Dictionary membership
questions.prompt: Given `student = {"name": "Ada", "credits": 15}`, what does `"Ada" in student` check?
choices: It checks whether `"Ada"` is a key in the dictionary.
It checks whether `"Ada"` is any value in the dictionary.
It checks both keys and values at the same time.
It checks whether every key has the value `"Ada"`.
questions.explanation: The `in` operator checks dictionary keys by default. In this example, `"name" in student` is true, while `"Ada" in student` is false unless `"Ada"` is also used as a key. To search values, use a values view or a different data shape.

questions.title: Choosing dictionary keys
questions.prompt: A gradebook stores one score per course code. What makes a good dictionary key?
choices: A value that changes every time the score changes.
A stable label such as the course code.
A duplicate label reused for several unrelated courses.
A list of all scores, because lists are easier to update.
questions.explanation: A key should identify the thing being looked up. A course code such as `"CS101"` is stable and descriptive, so the score can change without changing how the entry is found. Reusing one key for unrelated meanings causes updates to overwrite old values.

questions.title: Direct key access
questions.prompt: When is `student["email"]` the right lookup style?
choices: When missing email should quietly return an empty string.
When the code should search every value for an email address.
When the key is required and a missing key should be treated as an error.
When the dictionary might be empty and no error should happen.
questions.explanation: Square-bracket lookup is strict: if the key is absent, Python raises a KeyError. That is useful when missing data means something is wrong and should be fixed. If the field is optional, `get` with a fallback is usually clearer.

questions.title: Optional dictionary values
questions.prompt: A campus profile may or may not have a `"nickname"` field. Which lookup handles that safely?
choices: Use `profile["nickname"]` and hope the key exists.
Loop over every key even though the field name is known.
Treat a missing key as if it always means an empty dictionary.
Use `profile.get("nickname", "")` to supply a fallback.
questions.explanation: `get` is built for optional keys. It returns the stored value when the key exists and the fallback when it does not. That keeps expected missing data from turning into a KeyError while still making the fallback visible in the code.

questions.title: Looping over pairs
questions.prompt: A loop needs both each course code and its credit count. Which dictionary view fits?
choices: Use `.items()` so each loop step receives a key-value pair.
Use `.keys()` and pretend each key also contains the value.
Use `.values()` and try to recover the missing key later.
Use `len(dictionary)` because it returns all pairs.
questions.explanation: `.items()` produces pairs, so `for course, credits in courses.items():` gives both pieces at once. Iterating over the dictionary by itself gives only keys, and `.values()` leaves out the labels needed to know which course each credit count belongs to.

questions.title: Updating one key
questions.prompt: What happens when code assigns a new value to a key that already exists?
choices: The dictionary keeps both old and new values under duplicate keys.
The existing key stays once, and its value is replaced.
Python raises a duplicate-key error before assignment.
The key is removed because dictionaries cannot update values.
questions.explanation: A dictionary can hold each key only once. Assigning to an existing key updates the value for that key instead of adding a second copy. This is why counting and accumulation code must read the old value before replacing it with the updated total.
